claims.claim: Change management is the structured approach to moving an organization from a current state to a desired future state: SHRM defines change management as the systematic approach and application of knowledge, tools, and resources to deal with change and stresses that effective change management involves leading the 'people side' of major change, while OpenStax 10.2 defines planned change as intentional activity designed to create movement toward a specific goal or end; the lesson's working definition is attributed to these two sources.

Change is difficult and people often resist it; the deeper reason, per OpenStax 10.3's account of Kurt Lewin's model, is that most people prefer a stable, predictable organization and become accustomed to the routines around them, so existing norms, routines, and practices must be disrupted before change can happen.

OpenStax 10.2 defines incremental change as small refinements in current organizational practices or routines that do not challenge but rather build on or improve existing aspects (LEAN and Six Sigma given as common practices), and transformational change as significant shifts in an organizational system that may cause significant disruption to some underlying aspect of the organization, its processes, or structures (large systems changes and restructuring given as examples).

John Kotter, a Harvard Business School professor, developed a well-known and widely adopted eight-step model for managing organizational change: create a sense of urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a strategic vision, communicate the vision, remove obstacles, generate short-term wins, consolidate improvements, and anchor the changes in the culture (SHRM names Kotter and details eight stages; OpenStax 10.3 details all eight steps).

In Kotter's model as detailed by OpenStax 10.3, the first step (establishing a sense of urgency) means creating a narrative about why change is necessary, the fourth step means communicating the vision to all members of the organization and answering questions, the fifth step (removing obstacles) is intended to reduce resistance and provide resources, and the sixth step (creating small wins) signals to the organization that change is possible.

Employees often resist change when they have had no hand in shaping the plans or when they do not fully comprehend the urgency of the change or the vision for the change (OpenStax 10.3); SHRM's general practice for responding includes visible senior sponsorship, involving front-line managers early, training and regular communication, coaching employees to adapt, and rewarding desired behaviors, and OpenStax adds that removing obstacles reduces resistance.

Communication is central to leading change: Kotter's model makes communicating the vision a named step (OpenStax 10.3), and SHRM advises communicating in multiple forms and from multiple sources with repetition, cites a Robert Half survey in which 65 percent of managers called clear and frequent communication the most important aspect when leading through change, and states that effective communication strategies can double employees' acceptance of change.

Effective change management leads the 'people side' of major change and successful change starts with individuals (SHRM); OpenStax 10.3's account of Lewin's model frames change as routines and behaviors having to shift — supporting the lesson's honest framing that change is managed in the minds of the people and a plan is not a change until people accept and act on it.

Leadership copes with change — setting direction, aligning people, and motivating and inspiring — while management copes with complexity through planning and budgeting, organizing and staffing, and controlling and problem solving; the two are complementary (Kotter, What Leaders Really Do, HBR).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many steps the classic change model has
positions: Kotter's original model has eight steps: urgency, guiding coalition, strategic vision, communicate the vision, remove obstacles, short-term wins, consolidate improvements, anchor the changes (OpenStax 10.3; SHRM's eight stages).
SHRM also describes an alternative four-phase process (define, plan, implement, sustain) used by a large global retailer.

This lesson presents a five-move simplification — create urgency, build support, communicate, enable, sustain — explicitly labeled as a grouping of Kotter's eight steps in the Kotter tradition, not as a competing model.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The five-move version is presented as a teaching simplification of Kotter's eight-step model; the sources are cited for the eight-step original, and the lesson text states the simplification explicitly.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). openstax.org blocks direct fetching; verified via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20200930032926/ of the canonical section URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: types of change (structural, technological, culture); the dimensions of change (scope, level, intentionality); incremental change defined as small refinements in current practices or routines that build on rather than challenge existing aspects (LEAN and Six Sigma as common practices; incremental change does not typically push people to the edge of their comfort zone); transformational change defined as significant shifts in an organizational system that may cause significant disruption to underlying processes or structures (large systems changes and organizational restructuring as examples; can be invigorating for some employees but highly disruptive and stressful for others); planned change defined as intentional activity designed to create movement toward a specific goal or end, often involving large groups of people and step-by-step activities; unplanned change as unintentional and the result of informal organizing. Facts restated in original prose; the book's footer states it may not be used to train or be ingested into LLMs without permission, so usage is REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 10.3: Managing Change
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified via Wayback Machine capture (2020-09) of the canonical section URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: Lewin's change model — unfreezing (existing norms, routines, and practices must be disrupted), introducing changes that shift the system to a new state or reality, and refreezing (reinforcing new norms and practices); the observation that many people prefer a stable, predictable organization and become accustomed to existing routines; Kotter's change model as one of the most widely used in organizations today, an eight-step, centralized, top-down model: establish a sense of urgency (creating a narrative about why change is necessary; 'create a burning platform'), form a powerful guiding coalition, create a vision of change, communicate the vision (reach all members, explain why, answer questions), remove obstacles (reduce resistance, provide resources), create small wins, consolidate improvements, anchor the changes (new norms standardized; mode moves from transformational to incremental); the challenge that many employees resist change when they have had no hand in shaping the plans or do not fully comprehend the urgency or the vision; the conventional mindset that assumes people are inclined to resist change and need to be managed toward acceptance; Appreciative Inquiry and Complex Adaptive Systems as bottom-up alternatives. Facts restated in original prose (REFERENCE_ONLY).

sourceRecords.title: Managing Organizational Change (SHRM Toolkit)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A/B (SHRM is listed as Tier A/B in the subject source-map; professional HR association toolkit). Live fetch on 2026-08-22 returned the navigation shell only (article body JavaScript-rendered); full article read via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20240521123540/ on 2026-08-22. Supports: change management defined as the systematic approach and application of knowledge, tools and resources to deal with change; effective change management going beyond project management and technical tasks to lead the 'people side' of major change; the primary goal as successfully implementing new processes, products and business strategies while minimizing negative outcomes; 'Change is a fact of life in businesses today. It can be difficult, and people often resist it'; failure often occurring because of human nature and reluctance to change; John Kotter, a Harvard Business School professor, as the developer of a well-known and widely adopted eight-stage approach (urgency, guiding coalition, strategic vision, volunteer army/communication, removing barriers, short-term wins, sustaining acceleration, instituting change); an alternative four-phase process (define, plan, implement, sustain); employee resistance as a common obstacle with readiness states (indifference, rejection, doubt, neutrality, experimentation, commitment) and leader responses (senior sponsorship, involving front-line managers early, training, coaching, rewarding desired behaviors); communication breakdown as a common obstacle — Robert Half survey: 65 percent of managers cited clear and frequent communication as the most important aspect when leading through change; communicating in multiple forms and from multiple sources with repetition; experts estimating effective communication strategies can double employees' acceptance of change; HR's role in readiness assessment, training, and tracking adoption. Copyrighted; facts restated in original prose with no quoted text.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (professional education provider). Verified via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20240305051900/ on 2026-08-22 (live URL resolves but the article's predecessor resources URL now 404s). Supports: many change initiatives encounter failure or delay in achieving their goals; leaders need knowledge and tools to understand the factors that cause organizational change and how to lead teams through implementation; the importance of communication in successfully implementing change ('Without great communication, the change is destined to fail'); Kotter's 8-step model and other structured approaches for planning and delivering change; identifying the personal sources of resistance to organizational change; change requiring swift adaptation and continuous acquisition of new knowledge. Corroborates the Kotter attribution and the communication-in-change claim. Copyrighted; facts restated in original prose.
